It is not preference-based learning applied to audio clips, and the domain/modality is not audio as required by the topic definition.

evidence_ledger.quote: Scalable and efficient comparison-based search without features

support_spans.quote: We consider the problem of finding a target object t using pairwise comparisons, by asking an oracle questions of the form “Which object from the pair (i, j) is more similar to t?”. Objects live in a space of latent features, from which the oracle generates noisy answers. First, we consider the non-blind setting where these features are accessible. We propose a new Bayesian comparison-based search algorithm with noisy answers; it has low computational complexity yet is efficient in the number of queries. We provide theoretical guarantees, deriving the form of the optimal query and proving almost sure convergence to the target t. Second, we consider the blind setting, where the object features are hidden from the search algorithm. In this setting, we combine our search method and a new distributional triplet embedding algorithm into one scalable learning framework called LEARN2SEARCH....

The paper focuses on ordinal regression vs classification/regression for speech/affective computing datasets. Evidence shows ordinal scales and loss transitions, but no preference learning via ranking/A-B comparisons between audio clips and no RL preference-learning loop. Therefore it is outside the preference-based learning in audio criterion.

support_spans.quote: Many affective computing datasets are annotated using ordinal scales, as are many other forms of ground truth involving subjectivity, e.g. depression severity. When investigating these datasets, the speech processing community has chosen classification problems in some cases, and regression in others, while ordinal regression may also arguably be the correct approach for some. However, there is currently essentially no guidance on selecting a suitable machine learning and evaluation method. To investigate this problem, this paper proposes a neural network-based framework which can transition between different modelling methods with the help of a novel multi-term loss function. stage2_output.decision_rationale: Recall compiler final=include; model apparent=include; hard_exclusion=False. The paper trains a deep neural network metric using human judgments from comparing two audio recordings (identical vs different), via an iterative dataset/learning framework. It is applied to audio/perceptual differences (including speech telecommunication) and is not a survey/review. This matches preference-based learning with pairwise audio comparisons and a learning component.
